cue: How do you say wherever you end up, something stays true?

es.literal: to where it may want that you go
es.meaning: Wherever you go; in whatever place you find yourself.
es.example: A donde quiera que vayas, vas a encontrar a alguien que te recuerde a casa.
es.exampleTranslation: Wherever you go, you'll find someone who reminds you of home.

it.meaning: Wherever you go; in whatever place you find yourself.
it.example: Ovunque tu vada, porta con te questa abitudine.
it.exampleTranslation: Wherever you go, take this habit with you.

bridge.note: Both languages send the verb into the subjunctive and both mean exactly the same thing, so the lesson is not in the meaning — it is in what each language has to spell out. Spanish builds a small machine to get there: a donde + quiera + que + vayas, four words of scaffolding, and the ending on vayas already says who is going. Italian needs one word, ovunque — but then it needs a pronoun Spanish can leave out, because Italian's subjunctive vada is identical for I, you and he. Drop the tu and nobody knows whose journey it is.

interference.es_to_it: Keep the pronoun. Spanish drops subject pronouns as a matter of course and the habit is hard to break, but 'ovunque vada' leaves the person ambiguous — Italian wants 'ovunque TU vada'. And do not rebuild the Spanish scaffolding: there is no Italian equivalent of the quiera que frame.
interference.it_to_es: Spanish does not need the pronoun and adding it sounds heavy — 'a donde quiera que tú vayas' is possible but marked. Note the spelling too: 'adondequiera que vayas' written as one word is also correct, which surprises learners who have only seen it split.
